content: Monogenic diabetes syndromes, as classified by the American Diabetes Association (ADA), include specific types with distinct genetic and clinical characteristics. Neonatal Diabetes: This condition manifests in infants under six months of age and is frequently associated with specific genetic mutations. Neonatal diabetes can be categorized as either transient or permanent. Transient Neonatal Diabetes: This form is often caused by overexpression of genes located on chromosome 6q24. In some cases, it can be managed with medications other than insulin. However, it has the potential to recur later in life. Mutations in the KCNJ11 or ABCC8 genes are also implicated in this condition. Permanent Neonatal Diabetes: This form typically requires treatment with insulin. However, in certain cases, high-dose sulfonylureas may be effective as an alternative therapy. Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY): MODY is generally diagnosed before the age of 25 and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. It is characterized by impaired insulin secretion rather than insulin resistance and has minimal impact on body weight. Different subtypes of MODY are associated with mutations in specific genes. GCK-MODY (MODY 2): This subtype is marked by stable, mild hyperglycemia. It usually does not require pharmacological treatment, except during pregnancy. HNF1A-MODY (MODY 3) and HNF4A-MODY (MODY 1): Patients with these subtypes often respond well to low-dose sulfonylureas. Genetic testing is essential for accurate diagnosis and management, as it helps avoid unnecessary insulin use.
